item.content:encoded:
The Schuman Challenge is an annual academic competition organized by the Delegation of the European Union to the United States for undergraduate students enrolled at colleges and universities across the United States. The competition gives students the opportunity to conduct original research, develop practical policy recommendations on transatlantic issues, and present and defend their ideas before a panel of judges.

Registration for the 2027 edition is now open.

The Schuman Challenge is designed to encourage undergraduate students to engage with major issues affecting relations between the European Union and the United States. Through research, teamwork, policy analysis, public speaking and critical thinking, participants are challenged to examine a specific topic selected by the EU Delegation and develop actionable recommendations.

For students interested in international relations, political science, diplomacy, European studies, foreign policy, international security, economics, technology, public policy and transatlantic affairs, the Schuman Challenge provides an opportunity to apply academic knowledge to a real-world policy question.

About the Schuman Challenge

The Schuman Challenge is the annual foreign affairs contest organized by the European Union Delegation to the United States.

The competition focuses on EU-U.S. relations and asks participating undergraduate teams to develop policy recommendations addressing a specific topic announced by the EU Delegation.

Rather than simply writing an academic paper, participants must be prepared to present, explain and defend their recommendations before judges.

What Participants Are Expected to Do

Each participating team is expected to:

  1. Conduct original research on the competition topic.
  2. Examine relevant evidence and sources.
  3. Develop actionable policy recommendations.
  4. Prepare a 10-minute presentation.
  5. Present the proposal to a panel of judges.
  6. Participate in a 10-minute question-and-answer session.
  7. Defend the team’s recommendations and respond to questions from the judges.

The competition therefore combines academic research, policy analysis, teamwork, public speaking, critical thinking and communication skills.

Schuman Challenge 2027 Registration

Registration for the 2027 edition of the Schuman Challenge is now open.

The competition is organized specifically for undergraduate students at U.S. colleges and universities. Each participating institution can enter one team consisting of three to four undergraduate students.

Prospective participants should carefully review the official registration requirements and any updated competition guidance before registering.

2027 Application Deadline

The official page provided states that registration for the 2027 edition is open, but it does not currently state a specific closing deadline.

Applicants should therefore monitor the official registration page and the EU Delegation’s Schuman Challenge webpage for updates regarding the application deadline, competition topic and detailed 2027 requirements.

How the Schuman Challenge Works

The competition is structured around several stages that give participating teams the opportunity to progress from an online preliminary round to an in-person competition in Washington, D.C.

1. University or College Registration

The Schuman Challenge operates on a university and college team basis.

Only one team from each university or college can compete.

Each team consists of three to four undergraduate students.

Students interested in participating should therefore coordinate with their institution and determine how their university or college will organize its team.

2. Preliminary Round

The preliminary round takes place online in a live format.

Participating teams present their proposals to a panel of three judges.

The preliminary rounds are held on multiple dates.

During this stage, teams are expected to demonstrate their understanding of the assigned issue, explain their recommendations clearly and respond effectively to questions from the judges.

3. Semi-Final Round in Washington, D.C.

Fifteen teams qualify from the preliminary round and are invited to participate in the semi-final stage.

The semi-final takes place in person at the EU Delegation’s office in Washington, D.C.

The selected teams present their proposals to EU officials and experts.

Semi-finalist teams receive a travel stipend and accommodation in Washington, D.C., according to the competition information.

4. Final Round

Three teams progress from the semi-final stage to the final round.

The final round also takes place in Washington, D.C.

The finalist teams present their proposals and compete for the opportunity to become the winning team of the Schuman Challenge.

The Schuman Challenge Presentation Format

Each team gives a 10-minute presentation followed by a 10-minute question-and-answer session with the judges.

Visual aids may be used during the presentation.

This means participants need to be able to communicate complex policy issues in a clear and structured manner while also responding to questions under pressure.

The presentation should demonstrate the team’s understanding of the issue, the evidence supporting its position and the practical nature of its recommendations.

Research Requirements

Participants are expected to conduct original research, cite sources and prepare policy proposals based on credible evidence.

Teams Should Be Prepared To:

  • Identify the central policy challenge.
  • Research the existing EU-U.S. relationship relating to the issue.
  • Examine relevant evidence and existing policies.
  • Identify challenges, gaps or opportunities.
  • Develop an actionable policy recommendation.
  • Support their proposal with credible sources.
  • Prepare a structured presentation.
  • Anticipate questions from the judges.
  • Defend their recommendations during the Q&A session.

The Winning Team’s Prize

The winning team receives a four-day Victory Tour of Brussels, the headquarters of the European Union.

During the Victory Tour, the winning students have the opportunity to visit EU institutions and engage with officials and organizations involved in European policymaking.

The winning team also has the opportunity to present its winning policy proposal to EU officials.

What the Victory Tour Can Include

The prize provides the winning students with opportunities to:

  • Visit European Union institutions.
  • Meet or engage with EU officials.
  • Visit relevant organizations and think tanks.
  • Present their winning policy proposal.
  • Gain exposure to European policymaking.
  • Learn more about EU-U.S. relations and transatlantic cooperation.

The 2026 Schuman Challenge

The 2026 edition of the Schuman Challenge took place on April 7–8, 2026, at the EU Delegation’s office in Washington, D.C.

The 2026 competition focused on the future of EU-U.S. cooperation on security.

The competition topic asked students to develop a policy proposal analyzing the current state of EU-U.S. cooperation on security and proposing an initiative or policy that could strengthen the partnership in the coming years.

2026 Competition Areas

Teams were required to consider two of four areas:

  • Defense
  • Economy, trade and energy
  • Technology and digital
  • Arctic cooperation

The topic was connected to the 250th anniversary of the signing of the U.S. Declaration of Independence and the evolution of the transatlantic relationship.

2026 Participation and Results

The 2026 edition involved universities from across the United States.

According to the EU Delegation:

  • 34 universities participated in the preliminary rounds.
  • The participating universities represented 20 U.S. states and Washington, D.C.
  • 15 teams advanced to the semi-final round.
  • Three teams advanced to the final round.

2026 Final Results

  1. Macalester College, Minnesota
  2. Patrick Henry College, Virginia
  3. Stanford University, California

Macalester College won the 2026 competition.

The winning team developed a proposal called the “Atlantic Cable Infrastructure Program.” The proposal focused on cooperation between the European Union and United States to monitor, maintain and defend transatlantic cable systems using new technology.

The second- and third-placed teams were also commended for their policy proposals.

Skills Students Can Develop

The Schuman Challenge provides participants with an opportunity to develop practical skills that can be useful in academic, policy, diplomatic and professional environments.

Research Skills

Students conduct original research and use credible sources to support their recommendations.

Policy Analysis

Participants examine complex international issues and develop practical policy proposals.

Public Speaking

Each team must deliver a 10-minute presentation before judges.

Critical Thinking

Participants need to analyze the assigned issue and respond to questions about their recommendations.

Teamwork

Teams consist of three to four students, requiring participants to coordinate research, writing, presentation preparation and responses.

Communication

Students must explain complicated international policy issues in a clear and understandable manner.

International Affairs

The competition provides students with exposure to issues involving EU-U.S. relations, foreign affairs and transatlantic cooperation.

Who Should Consider This Opportunity?

The Schuman Challenge may be particularly relevant to undergraduate students interested in fields such as:

  • Political Science
  • International Relations
  • International Affairs
  • Diplomacy
  • European Studies
  • Foreign Policy
  • Security Studies
  • International Economics
  • Technology Policy
  • Public Policy
  • Government
  • International Development
  • Strategic Studies

However, the competition is not limited to one specific academic discipline. The key requirement is that participants meet the official eligibility requirements and can contribute effectively to their university’s team.

Important Eligibility Information

The Schuman Challenge is specifically designed for undergraduate students from U.S. colleges and universities.

Each university or college may enter only one team.

Teams consist of three to four undergraduate students.

Geographic Eligibility

The official competition description identifies undergraduate students from colleges and universities in the United States as the target participants.

Students studying at universities outside the United States should not assume that they are eligible simply because they are undergraduate students.

The competition is therefore not presented as an open worldwide opportunity for undergraduate students.

Benefits of Participating

Participating in the Schuman Challenge can provide students with several valuable experiences, including:

  • Opportunity to conduct original policy research.
  • Experience developing actionable policy recommendations.
  • Opportunity to present before judges and experts.
  • Exposure to EU officials and experts.
  • Experience participating in an academic foreign affairs competition.
  • Travel opportunity for qualifying teams to Washington, D.C.
  • Travel stipend and accommodation for semi-finalist teams.
  • Opportunity for the winning team to travel to Brussels.
  • Opportunity to visit EU institutions.
  • Opportunity to present to EU officials.
  • Development of teamwork and leadership skills.
  • Development of public speaking and presentation skills.
  • Exposure to transatlantic policy issues.

How to Prepare for the Schuman Challenge 2027

Students and universities interested in participating can begin preparing by taking the following steps.

Step 1: Form a Team

Identify three or four eligible undergraduate students who can work effectively together.

Step 2: Coordinate With Your University

Since only one team can represent each university or college, students should communicate with the relevant department, faculty, international affairs office or university administration about participation.

Step 3: Follow the Official 2027 Topic

The competition topic is determined by the EU Delegation. Teams should carefully study the official 2027 instructions once the topic and competition guide are available.

Step 4: Conduct Original Research

Use credible academic, governmental and institutional sources to understand the issue and the existing EU-U.S. relationship.

Step 5: Develop an Actionable Policy Proposal

Teams should develop a practical proposal rather than simply describing a problem.

Step 6: Prepare for Questions

Judges will have the opportunity to question participants, so teams should anticipate possible challenges to their recommendations.

Step 7: Practice the Presentation

The 10-minute presentation limit means teams should practice extensively to ensure that their most important arguments are presented clearly within the allotted time.

Registration Status

Application Deadline

Application Link

Interested eligible students and universities can access the official 2027 registration portal below:

-School-Registration-1

Official Website

For official information about the Schuman Challenge, competition updates, eligibility requirements and announcements from the European Union Delegation to the United States, visit:

schuman-challenge

OFY Website

For more opportunities for young people, visit the Opportunities For Youth website HERE

Conclusion

The Schuman Challenge 2027 is an academic competition that gives undergraduate students at U.S. colleges and universities an opportunity to engage with important issues concerning the European Union and the United States.

The competition combines original research, policy analysis, teamwork, public speaking and the development of actionable recommendations. Participants begin with an online preliminary stage, while successful teams can progress to an in-person competition in Washington, D.C.

Fifteen teams advance to the semi-final stage, three teams reach the final, and the winning team receives a four-day Victory Tour of Brussels, where students can visit EU institutions and present their winning proposal to EU officials.

With registration for the 2027 edition now open, eligible undergraduate students and U.S. universities can begin preparing their teams.

Because the official page provided does not currently state a 2027 registration deadline, prospective participants should regularly check the official Schuman Challenge website and registration portal for the latest deadline, competition topic, guide and application requirements.

item.content:encoded:
The White Rose Doctoral Training Partnership (WRDTP) has announced its call for nominations for ESRC studentship funding for doctoral research students commencing their studies in October 2027.

The funding provides an opportunity for prospective PhD researchers to undertake doctoral study in a wide range of social science disciplines at participating universities in the United Kingdom. Depending on the applicant’s previous academic and research training, successful candidates may receive funding through different award structures, including doctoral programmes that incorporate a research-training master’s year.

The WRDTP brings together seven partner universities and supports high-quality doctoral research addressing important social, economic and interdisciplinary issues.

Prospective applicants should note that the number of studentships advertised for the 2027 intake is currently provisional because ESRC Doctoral Training Partnerships are undergoing a mid-term review during 2026. The final number of available awards may therefore be adjusted following the review.

What Is the WRDTP ESRC Studentship?

The White Rose Doctoral Training Partnership is a doctoral training partnership that provides funding and research training for postgraduate researchers working in the social sciences.

The Economic and Social Research Council (ESRC) is one of the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) research councils and supports research and postgraduate training in the social sciences.

The WRDTP offers studentships at seven partner universities:

  1. University of Bradford
  2. University of Hull
  3. University of Leeds
  4. Manchester Metropolitan University
  5. University of Sheffield
  6. Sheffield Hallam University
  7. University of York

Applicants do not apply directly to the WRDTP for funding. Instead, candidates apply for an eligible PhD programme at one of the partner universities and are subsequently nominated by their university for WRDTP studentship consideration.

What Does the ESRC Studentship Fund?

The WRDTP provides several categories of doctoral studentships for students beginning their research degrees in October 2027.

These include:

1. WRDTP Pathway Awards

Pathway Awards support applicants who develop their own doctoral research proposals.

These awards are intended for impactful social science research that engages with key themes and challenges identified through the WRDTP’s interdisciplinary pathways.

Successful candidates undertake their research under the supervision of academic experts whose research interests align with the proposed doctoral project.

The Pathway Awards include interdisciplinary research opportunities and other specialist awards.

2. Advanced Quantitative Methods Awards

The Advanced Quantitative Methods (AQM) Awards support doctoral research involving advanced quantitative research methods.

These awards are particularly relevant to candidates whose proposed research requires sophisticated quantitative approaches to investigate social science questions.

Applicants interested in research involving statistical analysis, quantitative modelling, large datasets or other advanced quantitative methodologies may find this pathway particularly relevant.

3. Advanced Data Analytics Awards

The Advanced Data Analytics (ADA) Awards support doctoral projects involving advanced data analytics within the social sciences.

These awards are particularly relevant to research involving data-intensive approaches and analytical techniques.

Candidates considering research at the intersection of social science and data analytics should examine the specific eligibility and application requirements of the relevant department.

4. WRDTP Collaborative Awards

Collaborative Awards are different from the student-led Pathway, AQM and ADA awards.

Collaborative projects are designed by academic colleagues at WRDTP partner universities in collaboration with partners from sectors such as:

  • Private-sector organisations
  • Public-sector organisations
  • Third-sector organisations
  • Other external partners

Students can subsequently apply for studentships connected to the available collaborative projects.

This structure provides doctoral researchers with an opportunity to conduct research involving external organisations and real-world research challenges.

5. WRDTP/Stuart Hall Foundation Awards

The WRDTP also includes specialist awards delivered in collaboration with the Stuart Hall Foundation.

According to the current WRDTP eligibility information, these awards are specifically open to Black British students, including applicants identifying as Black or Black British African, Black or Black British Caribbean, Black or Black British other, or Mixed Black or Black British.

However, international students are not eligible for the WRDTP/Stuart Hall Foundation Awards.

How Long Does the WRDTP PhD Funding Last?

The WRDTP structures its awards according to the applicant’s previous academic qualifications and research training.

There are three principal programme structures.

+3.5 Programme

This provides funding for a 3.5-year PhD.

It is generally intended for applicants who already have a social science master’s degree and have completed approximately 60 or more credits, or an equivalent amount, of master’s-level social science research training.

This option is therefore particularly relevant to applicants who already have substantial postgraduate research training.

+3.75 Programme

This provides funding for an integrated PGCert/PhD programme lasting approximately 3.75 years.

It is generally intended for applicants who have a social science master’s degree but have not completed the required core research training.

The integrated structure enables the student to obtain additional research training before or alongside their doctoral research.

1+3.5 Programme

This provides funding for:

  • One year of master’s-level study; followed by
  • A 3.5-year PhD.

It is generally intended for applicants who do not already have a social sciences master’s degree.

This route may therefore be particularly important for graduates whose undergraduate degree is in a different field or who do not yet possess the postgraduate social science research training normally expected for direct doctoral entry.

Applicants are advised to select the appropriate structure according to their academic and research background and to discuss the choice with their proposed supervisor.

Who Can Apply?

The WRDTP ESRC studentships are intended for prospective doctoral researchers who want to undertake eligible social sciences PhD research at one of the WRDTP’s seven partner universities.

Applicants must satisfy both:

  1. The admission requirements of their chosen university, school or department; and
  2. The minimum eligibility requirements established for ESRC-funded studentships.

Applicants must hold an offer for a PhD place in an eligible school or department and intend to undertake a social science research project that falls within the ESRC’s remit.

The applicant’s proposed research must therefore be academically suitable for an eligible social science department and must fall within the relevant ESRC research scope.

Academic Qualification Requirements

The WRDTP states that applicants must meet the entry requirements of the school or department through which they are applying.

In addition, the ESRC requires studentship applicants to have qualifications equivalent to a good honours degree at first-class or upper-second-class level, or demonstrate equivalent ability through a combination of qualifications and/or experience.

Recognised equivalent international qualifications can be considered.

Applicants must satisfy the requirements of their chosen university as well as the ESRC’s minimum academic threshold.

Because individual universities and departments can impose additional requirements, prospective applicants should check the PhD entry requirements of their intended department before preparing their application.

Can International Students Apply?

Yes. International applicants can apply for WRDTP ESRC studentships, subject to the relevant eligibility requirements.

However, the WRDTP states that the ESRC limits the proportion of studentships available to international applicants to 30% of awards.

This means that international applicants can be considered, but the WRDTP cannot award more than 30% of its studentships to international candidates in a given year. Each partner university also has limits on the number of international candidates it can put forward.

Therefore, international applicants should contact their chosen department early to find out how that university manages the selection and nomination of international candidates.

For international students who are successfully awarded a standard WRDTP studentship, the WRDTP universities have agreed to cover the difference between the UK and international tuition fee rates. This means successful overseas students are not expected to personally pay the international fee gap.

However, the studentship does not cover costs such as visa fees, the Immigration Health Surcharge, flights or other expenses associated with moving to the United Kingdom.

Can Applicants from Africa Apply?

Yes. Applicants from African countries can be eligible to apply for the standard WRDTP ESRC studentships as international candidates, provided they meet the academic, university, departmental and ESRC requirements.

This means prospective applicants from countries such as Ghana, Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda and other eligible countries worldwide can potentially be considered.

Nationality alone does not guarantee eligibility. International candidates must obtain admission to an eligible PhD programme and must also go through the university’s nomination and selection process.

The 30% limit on international studentships is particularly important for applicants outside the UK.

Who Is Not Eligible?

Several restrictions apply.

Applicants Already Undertaking a PhD

Applicants who have already commenced a PhD are not eligible to apply for a WRDTP studentship, whether they are studying in the UK or internationally.

Applicants who have a PhD offer with a start date before 1 October 2027 should contact their university about possible deferral options. Deferring the start date may allow them to be considered for the 2027 WRDTP competition, subject to all other requirements.

Distance-Learning PhDs

Remote, online or distance-learning PhD programmes are not eligible for ESRC funding.

The funded study must be undertaken in accordance with WRDTP and ESRC requirements, including the requirement to reside within a reasonable travel distance of the university.

International Applicants for the Stuart Hall Foundation Award

Although international applicants can apply for standard WRDTP ESRC studentships, they are not eligible for the WRDTP/Stuart Hall Foundation Awards, which have specific eligibility criteria for Black British students.

Where Can Successful Applicants Study?

WRDTP studentships are available through eligible schools and departments at the partnership’s seven universities.

The partner universities are:

  • University of Bradford
  • University of Hull
  • University of Leeds
  • Manchester Metropolitan University
  • University of Sheffield
  • Sheffield Hallam University
  • University of York

Not every department at each university is necessarily eligible, so applicants should confirm that their proposed PhD department participates in the WRDTP.

For example, eligible departments include areas such as management, politics and international studies, law, sociology, social policy, education, geography, healthcare, psychology and other relevant disciplines, depending on the university.

Is Political Science Eligible?

Political and social science research can fall within the WRDTP’s remit where the proposed research is appropriate for an eligible department and falls within the ESRC’s scope.

For example, the University of Leeds lists its School of Politics and International Studies among its eligible departments.

Applicants with backgrounds in political science, public policy, international relations, development studies, sociology, economics, management and related fields should therefore investigate the specific PhD departments and research areas available at each partner university.

Eligibility ultimately depends on the proposed research, department, admission requirements and WRDTP/ESRC criteria.

What Does the Funding Cover?

WRDTP ESRC studentships provide substantial financial support for successful doctoral researchers.

The funding covers UK tuition fees and maintenance at the standard UKRI rate.

For international students, the WRDTP universities have agreed to cover the difference between UK and international tuition fees for studentship holders.

Students may also have access to additional funding opportunities during their studentship, including support connected with:

  • Research training
  • Overseas fieldwork
  • Difficult language training
  • Overseas institutional visits
  • Other approved research-related activities

The exact level of stipend is linked to the applicable UKRI rate for the relevant academic year and is revised periodically.

Applicants should therefore check the current UKRI rates when planning their finances.

Important Costs Not Covered

Although the studentship provides significant financial support, applicants should not assume that every cost associated with studying in the UK will be paid.

For international students in particular, the WRDTP states that UKRI studentship awards do not cover:

  • UK visa costs
  • Immigration Health Surcharge
  • Flights to or from the UK
  • Other relocation expenses

International applicants should therefore budget separately for these costs.

Application Deadline

The current WRDTP application guidance states that applicants must submit the following by:

Deadline: 17:00, 20 January 2027

Applicants must submit:

  1. An application for a PhD study place; and
  2. A WRDTP Studentship Application Form.

The studentship application is separate from the university’s ordinary PhD admission application.

Important: University Deadlines May Be Earlier

The 20 January 2027 deadline should not necessarily be treated as the first deadline an applicant needs to worry about.

Individual departments and schools may establish earlier internal deadlines so that they have sufficient time to review applications and determine which candidates they will nominate.

Applicants should therefore contact their preferred department as early as possible and confirm:

  • The PhD application deadline
  • The department’s internal WRDTP deadline
  • Supervisor requirements
  • Research proposal requirements
  • Any additional documents required
  • The university’s process for international applicants

The WRDTP does not accept direct applications from individual candidates. Universities nominate candidates to the WRDTP.

How the Application Process Works

The process generally involves several stages.

Step 1: Identify an Eligible University and Department

Choose one of the seven WRDTP partner universities and identify an eligible school or department that matches your proposed research.

Step 2: Develop Your Research Idea

Applicants seeking a Pathway, AQM or ADA studentship should develop a strong doctoral research proposal that aligns with the relevant research pathway and the expertise of potential supervisors.

Step 3: Find a Potential Supervisor

Applicants should contact potential supervisors and discuss their research proposal.

This is particularly important because the university, rather than the applicant, ultimately nominates candidates for WRDTP consideration.

Step 4: Apply for the PhD

Submit your PhD admission application to the chosen university according to its own requirements and deadline.

Step 5: Complete the WRDTP Studentship Application

Applicants must also complete the separate WRDTP Studentship Application Form.

Step 6: University Selection and Nomination

The university or department assesses applicants using its own fair and equitable process.

Successful candidates are nominated to the WRDTP for consideration.

Step 7: WRDTP Assessment

The WRDTP assesses the nominated candidates through its partnership-wide process.

Step 8: Funding Decision

Successful students are notified through their university.

The current WRDTP timetable indicates that nominations are submitted to the WRDTP by 17:00 on 24 February 2027, with assessment taking place during March 2027 and award winners expected to be announced by 23 April 2027.

What Kind of Research Can Be Funded?

The WRDTP focuses on social science research.

The Pathway Awards, for example, support student-led research projects that address important social science issues and engage with the WRDTP’s interdisciplinary research pathways.

Potential research areas can include subjects connected with:

  • Politics and government
  • Public policy
  • International relations
  • Economics
  • Sociology
  • Social policy
  • Education
  • Management
  • Geography
  • Law
  • Development
  • Healthcare and society
  • Data analytics
  • Quantitative social research
  • Other areas within the ESRC’s social science remit

The specific research topic must be compatible with the relevant university department and the ESRC’s remit.

Full-Time and Part-Time Study

The WRDTP states that its award structures are available for both full-time and part-time study.

However, applicants should carefully examine the requirements of their chosen university and department because the practical arrangements, duration and conditions can differ depending on the programme and mode of study.

Important Note About the 2026 ESRC DTP Review

The WRDTP has warned that all ESRC Doctoral Training Partnerships are undergoing a mid-term review in 2026.

Consequently, the number of studentships currently listed for the 2027 intake is provisional.

The number of awards could therefore change following the review.

Applicants should monitor the official WRDTP website and their chosen university for updates before submitting their application.

Key Information at a Glance

Information Details
Opportunity WRDTP ESRC Studentship Funding
Study level PhD / Doctoral Research
Start date October 2027
Main field Social Sciences
Funding organisation Economic and Social Research Council (ESRC) / UKRI
Programme White Rose Doctoral Training Partnership
Partner universities Bradford, Hull, Leeds, Manchester Metropolitan, Sheffield, Sheffield Hallam and York
Award structures +3.5, +3.75 and 1+3.5
Study mode Full-time or part-time
International applicants Eligible for standard WRDTP awards, subject to requirements
International award limit Maximum 30% of WRDTP awards
Tuition support UK tuition fees; WRDTP universities cover the international fee gap for eligible overseas students
Maintenance UKRI-standard maintenance stipend
PhD application deadline 17:00, 20 January 2027
WRDTP nomination deadline 17:00, 24 February 2027
Expected award announcement By 23 April 2027
PhD commencement October 2027

The dates above are based on the WRDTP’s current 2027 application guidance and should be checked again before applying because university departments may establish earlier deadlines.

Who Should Consider Applying?

This opportunity may be particularly relevant to:

  • Graduates seeking fully funded doctoral study in the UK
  • Social science researchers planning a PhD
  • Applicants with a social science master’s degree and research training
  • Applicants without a social science master’s degree who may qualify for the 1+3.5 route
  • Researchers interested in quantitative social science
  • Applicants interested in data analytics and social research
  • Researchers developing interdisciplinary projects
  • Applicants interested in collaborative research with external organisations
  • International students who meet the relevant UK university and ESRC requirements
  • Applicants from African and other countries seeking UK-funded doctoral study
  • Researchers interested in politics, public policy, development, management, sociology, economics, education, law and related fields

Advice for Prospective International Applicants

International applicants should begin preparing well before the January 2027 deadline.

A strong preparation strategy includes:

  1. Researching the seven WRDTP universities.
  2. Identifying eligible departments.
  3. Reviewing potential supervisors and their research interests.
  4. Developing a clear research proposal.
  5. Checking the university’s PhD entry requirements.
  6. Checking whether your international degree meets the required academic standard.
  7. Contacting the department about international applicant selection.
  8. Confirming the university’s internal deadline.
  9. Preparing academic transcripts and supporting documents.
  10. Completing the separate WRDTP studentship application.
  11. Planning for visa and relocation costs that are not covered by the studentship.
  12. Monitoring the WRDTP website for any changes following the 2026 ESRC DTP mid-term review.

Starting early is particularly important because applicants do not apply directly to the WRDTP. The university must first assess and nominate candidates.

Conclusion

The WRDTP ESRC Studentship Funding 2027 provides an important opportunity for prospective doctoral researchers seeking funded social science PhD study in the United Kingdom.

The programme offers several routes, including the +3.5 PhD, +3.75 integrated PGCert/PhD, and 1+3.5 master’s-plus-PhD pathway, allowing applicants to select a route that corresponds with their previous academic and research training.

The opportunity is open to eligible applicants from the UK and internationally, although international applicants are subject to the ESRC’s 30% limit on international studentship awards. Successful overseas students can benefit from the WRDTP universities’ commitment to covering the difference between UK and international tuition fees, although visa, Immigration Health Surcharge, travel and relocation expenses remain the student’s responsibility.

Prospective applicants should not wait until the final deadline to begin preparing. Because universities may set earlier internal deadlines and applicants must first go through the university’s nomination process, early contact with the relevant department and potential supervisor is essential.

For the current 2027 intake, the main WRDTP application deadline is 17:00 on 20 January 2027, while university departments may require applications earlier.

Applicants should carefully review the official WRDTP eligibility requirements, identify an eligible department, develop a suitable research proposal and follow the application process established by their chosen university.

item.content:encoded:
Are you a university student looking to launch your career with one of the world’s leading technology and payments companies? Mastercard is inviting eligible students across North America and Latin America to attend its upcoming Inside Mastercard: Interns & Launchers (Americas) information session.

This online event provides students with an opportunity to learn more about Mastercard’s internship and Launch Programs, explore career opportunities across technology, consulting, product, sales and data, and gain valuable insights directly from Mastercard employees and early-career professionals.

The session is designed to help students understand what it is like to work at Mastercard, how its early-career programs operate, what opportunities are available, and how applicants can prepare for the recruitment and interview process.

About the Mastercard Interns & Launchers Information Session

Mastercard is a global technology company operating at the intersection of payments, technology and innovation. Through its early-career programs, the company provides students and recent university talent with opportunities to gain professional experience, work on meaningful projects and contribute to solutions that affect consumers, businesses and governments around the world.

The Inside Mastercard: Interns & Launchers (Americas) event is an online information session focused on Mastercard’s Intern and Launch Programs across North America and Latin America.

During the session, participants will learn about the company’s early-career opportunities and hear directly from Mastercard professionals about their experiences.

The event will feature perspectives from a:

  • People Manager
  • Current Launcher
  • Program Buddy

These speakers will provide insight into their career journeys, experiences at Mastercard and what it is like to develop professionally within the organization.

What Will Participants Learn?

The information session is designed to give students a better understanding of Mastercard’s early-career opportunities and recruitment process.

Participants can expect to learn about:

1. Mastercard’s Intern and Launch Programs

Students will learn more about the company’s internship and Launch Programs, including how these opportunities can help students begin their professional careers and gain exposure to a global technology organization.

The programs are designed to give early-career talent the opportunity to work on meaningful projects and develop practical skills while working alongside experienced professionals.

2. Career Opportunities Across Multiple Fields

Mastercard offers early-career opportunities across a wide range of professional and technical disciplines.

Areas highlighted for the Americas programs include:

  • Consulting
  • Engineering
  • Software Engineering
  • Artificial Intelligence
  • Product Management
  • Sales
  • Data Science
  • Technology
  • Product Innovation
  • Data-driven decision-making
  • Other related areas

This means students with different academic and professional interests can explore potential career paths within Mastercard.

3. Firsthand Experiences From Mastercard Employees

One of the key features of the session is the opportunity to hear directly from people who have experience with Mastercard’s early-career environment.

A People Manager, Current Launcher and Program Buddy will share their experiences, career journeys and perspectives on professional growth at Mastercard.

These insights can help prospective applicants better understand the company beyond the information available on a traditional job posting.

4. Mastercard’s Culture and Work Environment

Participants will also learn about Mastercard’s culture and its focus on innovation, inclusion and professional growth.

The company emphasizes creating an environment where early-career professionals can contribute to meaningful work and make an impact from the beginning of their careers.

Students interested in joining a global technology company can use the session to understand Mastercard’s workplace culture and what the company looks for in early-career talent.

5. Application and Interview Tips

Another important part of the session is gaining insight into Mastercard’s application and recruitment process.

Participants can learn about:

  • How to approach the application process
  • Important recruitment timelines
  • What to expect during the interview process
  • Ways to make an application stand out
  • How students can better prepare for early-career opportunities
  • What Mastercard looks for in potential candidates

These insights can be particularly valuable for students preparing to apply for internships or full-time early-career opportunities.

Who Should Attend?

The Inside Mastercard: Interns & Launchers Americas session is intended for students who are actively exploring internship and full-time career opportunities.

The session is particularly relevant to students who are:

  • In their first, second or third year of a Bachelor’s degree
  • Pursuing an accelerated Master’s degree
  • Studying at a college or university in North America or Latin America
  • Interested in technology and innovation
  • Interested in consulting
  • Interested in product management
  • Interested in engineering or software
  • Interested in artificial intelligence
  • Interested in sales
  • Interested in data science
  • Interested in solving real-world problems
  • Interested in data-driven decision-making
  • Looking for internship opportunities
  • Exploring future full-time career opportunities

Students from different academic backgrounds may benefit from attending if their interests align with Mastercard’s areas of opportunity.

Areas of Opportunity at Mastercard

Mastercard’s early-career opportunities cover several disciplines, allowing students to explore different career paths within the organization.

Consulting

Students interested in business strategy, problem-solving and advising organizations can explore opportunities related to consulting.

Engineering and Technology

Engineering opportunities can include areas such as software engineering, technology development and artificial intelligence.

Students interested in building technology and developing innovative solutions may find these areas particularly relevant.

Product Management

Product management opportunities are suitable for students interested in developing products and solutions that address real-world customer and business needs.

Sales

Students interested in business development, client relationships and commercial strategy can explore sales-related career opportunities.

Data Science

Students interested in using data to solve problems and support decision-making can explore opportunities related to data science and analytics.

Why Consider a Career With Mastercard?

Mastercard provides early-career professionals with the opportunity to gain exposure to a global technology and payments organization.

Through its Intern and Launch Programs, participants can potentially gain experience working alongside industry professionals and contribute to projects that have real-world applications.

Some of the key reasons students may want to explore Mastercard’s early-career programs include:

  • Exposure to a global technology company
  • Opportunities to work alongside experienced professionals
  • Exposure to global projects
  • Opportunities to develop professional and technical skills
  • Exposure to technology, payments and innovation
  • Opportunities across multiple career disciplines
  • Learning about professional development within a global organization
  • The opportunity to contribute to solutions affecting consumers, businesses and governments
  • Exposure to an innovation-driven working environment

Event Format

The Inside Mastercard: Interns & Launchers Americas event will be held entirely online.

This makes it possible for eligible students across the relevant regions to participate without travelling to a physical venue.

Event Details

Event: Inside Mastercard: Interns & Launchers (Americas)

Format: Online Event

Date: Friday, September 25, 2026

Time: 2:00 PM – 3:00 PM EDT

Registration Deadline: September 20, 2026 at 11:59 PM EST

Students interested in attending should register before the deadline.

REGISTER HERE

Important Registration Instructions

Students should pay close attention to the registration process.

After completing the registration form, Mastercard requires participants to confirm their registration through an email sent after submitting the form.

The event details will not be provided unless the registration is confirmed.

Applicants should therefore:

  1. Complete the registration form before the deadline.
  2. Check the email address used during registration.
  3. Look for the registration confirmation email.
  4. Open the confirmation email and complete the required confirmation process.
  5. Check the spam or other folders if the confirmation email does not appear in the main inbox.

According to Mastercard, the confirmation email is sent from jobalert@careers.mastercard.com.

Students should make sure they do not overlook this confirmation step because simply completing the initial registration form does not guarantee that they will receive the event details.

Registration Deadline

The deadline to register for the Inside Mastercard: Interns & Launchers Americas information session is:

September 20, 2026 at 11:59 PM EST

Interested students are encouraged to register before the deadline rather than waiting until the final hours.

How the Event Can Help Students

Attending an early-career information session can help students understand what a company expects from prospective interns and early-career employees.

For students considering Mastercard, this event can provide useful information about available programs, career areas, recruitment timelines and interview preparation.

It can also help students determine which Mastercard opportunities best match their academic background, skills and career interests.

Students can use the information gained from the session to better prepare for future internship and Launch Program applications.

How to Prepare for the Mastercard Information Session

Students planning to attend can take several steps to make the most of the event.

Research Mastercard

Before attending, learn about Mastercard’s business, technology, products, culture and areas of innovation.

Having some background knowledge can make it easier to understand the information presented during the session.

Identify Your Career Interests

Think about which areas of Mastercard interest you most.

For example, you may be interested in:

  • Consulting
  • Software engineering
  • Artificial intelligence
  • Product management
  • Data science
  • Sales
  • Technology
  • Business strategy

Having a clear area of interest can help you focus on the information most relevant to your career goals.

Prepare Questions

Participants should consider preparing questions before the event.

Potential questions could cover internship responsibilities, Launch Program opportunities, recruitment timelines, required skills, interview preparation and professional development.

Watch Your Email

After registering, carefully monitor the email account used during registration.

The confirmation email is essential because Mastercard states that participants will not receive the event details unless they confirm their registration.

Geographic Eligibility

This particular Mastercard information session is designed for students across North America and Latin America.

The opportunity therefore has a regional focus on the Americas.

Students studying outside these regions should carefully review Mastercard’s other early-career programs and events to determine whether there are separate opportunities available for their location.

Important Note for International Students

The event should not be confused with a worldwide Mastercard internship application.

Although Mastercard is a global company, the event described here specifically focuses on its North America and Latin America Intern and Launch Programs.

Students should therefore verify their geographic eligibility before registering.

Where to Find More Information

Students can learn more about Mastercard’s early-career programs, career opportunities and recruitment process through the company’s official careers platform.

Mastercard also provides information about its hiring process, interview preparation, available positions, talent community and early-career programs.

Interested students should use the official Mastercard careers website for the most accurate and up-to-date information regarding eligibility, applications and recruitment.

Conclusion

The Inside Mastercard: Interns & Launchers (Americas) information session is an opportunity for eligible university students to learn more about starting a career with Mastercard and to gain firsthand insight into the company’s early-career programs.

The online session will cover Mastercard’s Intern and Launch Programs, career opportunities in consulting, engineering, software, artificial intelligence, product management, sales and data science, as well as the company’s culture and approach to professional development.

Participants will also hear from Mastercard professionals, including a People Manager, Current Launcher and Program Buddy, giving students an opportunity to gain practical insight into life and career development at the company.

Students interested in participating should register by September 20, 2026 at 11:59 PM EST and, importantly, confirm their registration through the email sent after submitting the registration form.

For eligible students across North America and Latin America who are interested in technology, consulting, product innovation, data, engineering or business, this session can be a useful opportunity to learn how to prepare for Mastercard’s internship and early-career recruitment opportunities.

Visit the OFY Website HERE for more global opportunities

item.content:encoded:
The Nuffield Foundation has launched the Essential Employment Skills Fund, a major new funding initiative offering grants of up to £500,000 to build robust evidence about how young people facing significant barriers to employment can develop the skills, attributes and behaviours needed to access and progress into good jobs.

The fund focuses specifically on young people aged 16–24 living in the United Kingdom who face significant barriers to entering the labour market. Rather than simply supporting skills programmes, the initiative seeks to establish high-quality evidence about which interventions work, why they work, for whom they work, and how successful approaches can ultimately be expanded or adapted to different settings.

The outline application deadline is 10 December 2026, according to the Nuffield Foundation’s announcement of the fund. Shortlisted applicants will subsequently be invited to submit full applications in 2027.

About the Nuffield Foundation Essential Employment Skills Fund

The Essential Employment Skills Fund has been established in response to a major challenge facing the UK: many young people, particularly those from disadvantaged backgrounds or facing substantial barriers to work, do not have equal opportunities to develop the skills that employers value.

The Nuffield Foundation argues that employment-related skills development needs to be more effectively integrated across education, training and youth-support systems. At the same time, these interventions need to be supported by stronger evidence about what actually works.

Through the new fund, the Foundation therefore aims to support the rigorous evaluation of existing UK programmes that help young people aged 16–24 develop essential employment skills and move toward good employment.

Grants of up to £500,000 are available for evaluation, with the Foundation anticipating that most evaluation awards will fall between approximately £200,000 and £400,000. There is also potential for additional support toward programme-delivery costs where those costs cannot be covered from other sources, including through partnership funding arrangements.

Why Has the Essential Employment Skills Fund Been Created?

Youth unemployment and economic inactivity represent serious long-term challenges.

Young people who struggle to enter the labour market or gain meaningful employment experience during early adulthood may face consequences extending far beyond their first few years of working life. These can affect their longer-term career trajectories, earnings and well-being.

At the same time, employers continue to report difficulties finding young people with the skills they need.

The Nuffield Foundation identifies an important disconnect: although employers and educators increasingly recognize the importance of essential employment skills, these competencies do not necessarily receive sufficient emphasis within curricula, assessment and accountability systems.

Opportunities to develop these skills can consequently vary substantially according to a young person’s circumstances and background.

The Essential Employment Skills Fund aims to address an important evidence gap: Which approaches actually help young people facing significant barriers to work develop essential employment skills and progress toward sustainable employment?

What Are Essential Employment Skills?

For this funding programme, the Nuffield Foundation uses “essential employment skills” as an inclusive term covering a broad range of transferable skills, attributes and behaviours valued by employers across industries and occupations.

These skills are associated with important labour-market outcomes such as gaining employment, progressing at work, job satisfaction and earnings.

The Foundation highlights research identifying areas such as:

  • Collaboration
  • Communication
  • Creative thinking
  • Information literacy
  • Organising, planning and prioritising
  • Problem solving
  • Decision making

Other established frameworks cover comparable competencies, including speaking, listening, creativity, adapting, planning, leadership and teamwork.

Applicants do not have to adopt one particular skills framework. They may use an appropriate existing framework that suits their programme.

However, proposals must clearly identify the specific essential employment skill or skills that the intervention intends to develop.

Importantly, the Fund is not intended to finance the creation of new definitions or frameworks for essential employment skills.

Main Aim of the Fund

The central purpose of the Essential Employment Skills Fund is to strengthen the evidence base concerning effective approaches for helping young people aged 16–24 who face significant employment barriers develop essential skills and ultimately gain access to good jobs.

The Nuffield Foundation intends to achieve this by supporting rigorous evaluations of relevant programmes and facilitating the dissemination of findings and practical learning.

The longer-term objective is not merely to determine whether individual projects succeed. The Foundation wants the evidence generated through funded projects to help successful practices be:

  • Expanded;
  • Replicated;
  • Adapted to different contexts;
  • Incorporated into wider education and employment systems; and
  • Used to reduce inequalities in young people’s employment outcomes.

The Foundation is also interested in projects that improve mechanisms for sharing learning or advance methods for measuring essential employment skills.

How Much Funding Is Available?

The Essential Employment Skills Fund offers substantial financial support.

Maximum grant for evaluation: Up to £500,000

The Foundation expects most evaluation grants to fall within the range of approximately:

£200,000 to £400,000

In appropriate circumstances, there may also be additional funding available to contribute toward programme-delivery costs when these cannot be funded from other sources.

Organizations considering requesting delivery funding are encouraged to contact the Nuffield Foundation before submitting their application to discuss the proposed arrangements.

Who Can Apply?

The Essential Employment Skills Fund is primarily designed around organizational partnerships rather than applications from individual young people.

This distinction is important.

The young people aged 16–24 are primarily the target beneficiaries of the programmes being evaluated, rather than individual applicants for the £500,000 grants.

For this particular fund, successful teams will require expertise in two major areas:

  1. Independent evaluation and research expertise
  2. Frontline programme delivery expertise

The Nuffield Foundation therefore anticipates receiving applications from partnerships between an evaluator/research organization and a delivery organization.

The partnership must already have been established before an application is submitted, and the research design should be developed jointly.

Applicants must also clearly explain the division of roles and responsibilities and demonstrate how the evaluation will retain sufficient independence and impartiality.

The Foundation expects the evaluation partner to act as the lead applicant.

Who Should the Programmes Support?

Funded programmes must work with young people aged 16–24 living in the UK, although applicants may choose to concentrate on a narrower age group within this range.

For example, an intervention could specifically target people aged 16–19.

However, the central emphasis must remain on young people who face significant barriers to employment.

Applicants are expected to clearly identify their intended target population and provide a persuasive justification for selecting that group.

Young People Facing Significant Barriers to Work

The Foundation identifies several circumstances that may increase the likelihood of a young person struggling to access employment.

Projects could, for example, focus on young people experiencing one or more factors such as:

  • Low or no academic qualifications;
  • Persistent absence from school;
  • School exclusion;
  • Special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), particularly young people with an Education, Health and Care Plan;
  • Mental health difficulties;
  • Experience of the care system;
  • Young parenthood;
  • Responsibilities as a young carer;
  • Membership of Gypsy, Roma or Traveller communities; or
  • Residence in geographic areas experiencing comparatively high youth unemployment.

These examples should not be interpreted as a requirement that every funded programme must cover every listed group.

Instead, applicants need to define their particular target population and provide evidence explaining why the selected group faces meaningful barriers to employment.

Reaching Young People Who Need Support Most

The Nuffield Foundation places particular emphasis on recruitment and sustained engagement.

Applicants must provide a realistic strategy explaining how they will:

  1. Identify eligible young people;
  2. Recruit them into the programme;
  3. Maintain their participation and engagement; and
  4. Avoid restricting participation to individuals who are comparatively easy to reach.

This is significant because programmes intended to reduce employment inequality can fail to achieve their purpose if they primarily attract individuals who are already comparatively well connected to education, training or employment services.

What Types of Programmes Can Be Funded?

An eligible programme must have an explicit objective of developing at least one essential employment skill among participating young people.

Many programmes will naturally address several skills simultaneously.

The development of essential employment skills may form part of a broader programme containing other forms of support.

Potential activities could include:

  • Literacy, numeracy or digital-skills development;
  • Vocational education or training;
  • CV preparation;
  • Interview preparation and employment support;
  • Enterprise and entrepreneurship training;
  • Mentoring;
  • Coaching;
  • Volunteering;
  • Community activities;
  • Work experience;
  • Work-based learning;
  • Peer support;
  • Mental-health support; and
  • Assistance with practical barriers such as housing or benefits.

This provides applicants with considerable flexibility in designing or adapting programmes, provided that essential employment skills remain an explicit and measurable component.

Existing and Promising Programmes Are Prioritized

Organizations should note that the Fund is not primarily designed to finance entirely new programmes developed from scratch.

Given the level of funding available and the emphasis on rigorous evaluation, the Nuffield Foundation expects to support existing programmes that already demonstrate some evidence of promise.

Projects may nevertheless adapt or refocus an established intervention.

For example, an organization could propose testing an existing programme within a different environment, population or delivery context.

The programme should be based on a clear and convincing theory of change, supported by previous testing, relevant evidence and/or theoretical literature.

Robust Impact Evaluation Is Essential

Evaluation is not an optional addition to this funding opportunity; it is one of its defining requirements.

Funded programmes must include a robust impact evaluation.

At minimum, the evaluation must examine:

  • Changes in the targeted essential employment skills; and
  • Participants’ progress toward employment.

Progress toward employment could include outcomes such as:

  • Starting a job;
  • Beginning an apprenticeship;
  • Accessing voluntary employment;
  • Participating in a supported internship;
  • Completing work experience; or
  • Enrolling in further training.

The appropriate evaluation methodology will depend on the intervention and its stage of development.

However, the Foundation expects sufficiently large samples for robust analysis and credible evidence that observed outcomes can be attributed to the programme rather than unrelated external factors.

Depending on the programme, this may require control or comparison groups or high-quality qualitative impact methodologies.

Process and Implementation Evaluation

Applicants must also include process and implementation evaluation.

This recognizes that even a well-designed programme may achieve different outcomes when delivered in different real-world environments.

Factors influencing implementation may include:

  • Organizational culture;
  • Stakeholder priorities;
  • Practical constraints;
  • Physical circumstances;
  • Government policy;
  • Regulation;
  • Local labour-market conditions; and
  • Wider political or institutional environments.

Evaluation should therefore examine not only whether an intervention works but also how it is implemented and what contextual factors influence its effectiveness.

Young People’s Voices Must Influence the Programme

The Fund also requires applicants to consider the contemporary experiences and perspectives of young people themselves.

Proposals should demonstrate how evidence from young people has informed—or will inform—the programme’s design and delivery.

Organizations may establish a youth advisory board or youth engagement group, although this specific structure is not compulsory.

What matters is that applicants can explain how young people’s own perspectives on employment barriers and potential solutions are incorporated meaningfully into the programme.

Partnership and Collaboration

Another important ambition of the Fund is to strengthen partnerships around youth employment.

Funded projects may bring together stakeholders including:

  • Employers;
  • Education institutions;
  • Training providers;
  • Third-sector organizations;
  • Research and evaluation organizations;
  • Local government; and
  • Regional government.

The Foundation hopes these collaborations can continue supporting young people beyond the lifespan of an individual funded project.

Support Available from the Nuffield Foundation

Potential applicants can seek feedback before submitting a formal application.

The Foundation welcomes a brief one-page project description from prospective applicants seeking initial feedback.

Delivery organizations that do not yet have an evaluation partner may also request information about potential evaluators who have agreed to be approached by applicants to the programme.

Successful projects will receive additional support from the Nuffield Foundation during implementation, including assistance relating to communications and impact.

The Foundation also intends to connect grant holders with other funded organizations and its wider stakeholder network, enabling organizations to exchange learning and promote effective practice.

Essential Employment Skills Fund Application Timeline

The current timetable is:

Outline application deadline: 10 December 2026

Shortlisting decisions: February 2027

Full application deadline: April 2027

Final funding decisions: July 2027

Earliest possible project start: September 2027

Applicants should also check the official funding page for updates and FAQs before finalizing their submissions.

How to Apply

Applicants must follow the Nuffield Foundation’s Outline Application process and carefully review the Foundation’s Guide for Applicants before submitting.

The Foundation expects the evaluation partner to be the lead applicant.

Prospective applicants should therefore establish their evaluator-delivery organization partnership before applying and jointly develop the proposed research and evaluation design.

Apply for the Nuffield Foundation Essential Employment Skills Fund

Why This Funding Opportunity Matters

The Essential Employment Skills Fund is particularly significant because it combines youth-employment intervention with rigorous evidence generation.

Many organizations already deliver employability, mentoring, training, work-experience and youth-development programmes. However, policymakers and practitioners need stronger evidence about which approaches produce measurable improvements, particularly for young people who are furthest from the labour market.

The Fund is therefore designed to move beyond simply financing individual interventions.

Its wider ambition is to generate knowledge capable of informing future education, training, youth-support and employment systems, allowing promising interventions to be improved, scaled or adapted.

The initiative also recognizes that employability is not determined solely by technical qualifications. Communication, collaboration, planning, creativity, problem solving, adaptability, teamwork and similar transferable competencies can play an important role in helping young people navigate an increasingly complex labour market.

Conclusion

The Nuffield Foundation Essential Employment Skills Fund 2026 represents a substantial funding opportunity for organizations working at the intersection of youth employment, education, training, research and programme evaluation in the United Kingdom.

With up to £500,000 available for evaluation, and potential additional support toward programme-delivery costs in appropriate circumstances, the Fund aims to generate robust evidence about how young people aged 16–24 who face significant employment barriers can develop essential skills and ultimately access good jobs.

Strong proposals will require more than an innovative idea. Applicants should have an established and promising intervention, a compelling theory of change, an appropriate target population, credible plans for reaching young people facing significant barriers, a strong independent evaluation design, meaningful engagement with young people’s perspectives, and an established partnership between frontline delivery and evaluation expertise.

Organizations considering applying should begin preparing well ahead of the 10 December 2026 outline application deadline, particularly because partnerships should be established and the research design co-developed before the application is submitted.
